newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-ITALIAN FLAIR TAKES ON GERMAN INDUSTRY IN UEFA FINAL.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ITALIAN FLAIR TAKES ON GERMAN INDUSTRY IN UEFA FINAL.

text.p: Italian flair will try to break down dogged German industry when Internazionale Milan meet Schalke in one of the most contrasting final line-ups in UEFA Cup history on Wednesday.
Rarely have two clubs with such different backgrounds come together for a European final.
Inter boast a history of international success while their German rivals have never won a European trophy. Even Schalke's last domestic triumph was back in 1972 when they won the German Cup.
The two legs will be played in cities which are also light years apart in terms of culture and atmosphere.

Gelsenkirchen, an unattractive industrial city in the Ruhr which has been hit hard by unemployment in recent years, will host the first leg before the second game in one of Europe's most fashionable cities in northern Italy in two weeks.

On paper the two teams are also in different classes. Despite the suspension of French defender Jocelyn Angloma, English midfielder Paul Ince and Frenchman Youri Djorkaeff for the first leg, the Italians are still a major force.

By contrast unglamorous Schalke have few top-class players who are known internationally apart from their key midfielder-cum-libero Olaf Thon, a former World Cup player, and Czechs Jiri Nemec and Radoslav Latal.

Inter will be looking to win the Cup for the third time after 1991 and 1994 but nobody should write off the Germans. One of the biggest factors in Schalke's favour in Gelsenkirchen's Parkstadium will be their fans.

Schalke were a major force in German football during the Second World War winning the championship six times between 1934 and 1942. But although their last German title came in 1958, they still have a fanatical following around the country.
Anybody who spends more than a hour on a German autobahn is almost certain to drive past at least one car boasting a blue plate with the club's name on the back window.

Schalke fans have never been afraid of demonstrating their allegiance. Their fans have a reputation for being emotional. Even when the club was relegated three times during the 1980s the club kept its following.

"They're one of the best supported clubs in the Bundesliga and it will be a tough game for us," Inter's English coach Roy Hodgson said. "Only a fool underestimates his opponent and only a fool takes comfort from past results".
Schalke coach Huub Stevens is hoping to have a fully fit squad apart from Dutch striker Youri Mulder who is out for the rest of the season.

Internazionale's English coach Roy Hodgson has called up two youth team players in 18-year defender Tiziano Polenghi and 19-year-old midfielder Sergio D'Autilia because of the suspensions and injuries.

Striker Maurizio Ganz and utility player Salvatore Fresi are suffering from influenza while Swiss midfielder Ciriaco Sforza is troubled by a long-term, leg injury. But, given the lack of alternatives, they are all expected to play.

"Physically, we're not in great condition and pride and willingness to sacrifice ourselves will count for a lot against a physically tough side", says Ganz, scorer of eight goals on the way to the final.
Schalke - Jens Lehmann, Olaf Thon, Johan de Kock, Thomas Linke, Radoslav Latal, Andreas Mueller, Jiri Nemec, Michael Bueskens, Ingo Anderbruegge, Marc Wilmots, Martin Max
Inter - Gianluca Pagliuca, Giuseppe Bergomi, Fabio Galante, Massimo Paganin, Alessandro Pistone, Javier Zanetti, Ciriaco Sforza, Salvatore Fresi, Aron Winter, Maurizio Ganz, Ivan Zamorano.
